**Before the visit**
- Add the visit date on the "Visit" tab. MenoMap shows how ready your notes are and what would make them more complete.
- Choose the topics and questions that matter most. Limit it to three or four.
- Create notes for the last 30 or 90 days. Check that your medication list is up to date.

**At the visit**
- Hand over or show the first page. It is made to be read in under a minute: counts, averages, a heat calendar and your questions.
- Start with the question that matters most to you.
- If your doctor speaks another language, you can create the notes in that language.

**What these notes are and are not**

This is a summary of what you entered, and also of everything you decided to bring over from the Health app. It is not a diagnosis and not complete medical records, and any patterns in them are a coincidence check, not proof of a cause. The doctor may ask questions the notes do not answer, and that is normal.

**After the visit**

Add the new medication with the date you started taking it. After a few weeks MenoMap will be able to show your records before and after, and this will make the next review of the treatment easier.
backTranslations.42:
**Menopause** is a single point in time: the day when 12 months in a row have passed without a period, if this is not explained by something else (for example pregnancy, certain medications or surgery). In many countries it happens on average shortly after age 50, but it often occurs at any age from roughly 45 to 55.

**Perimenopause** is the years leading up to that point. Hormone levels rise and fall unevenly, so periods can become irregular, heavier or lighter, more frequent or less frequent. Many changes that are linked with menopause, such as hot flushes, night sweats, sleep and mood changes, often begin exactly when periods are still continuing. Perimenopause can last several years or considerably longer, and in each person it passes in its own way.

**Postmenopause** is everything after the 12-month mark. Some symptoms subside over time, others can last for years.

Menopause can also occur earlier because of an operation to remove the ovaries, some cancer treatments or other health conditions. Menopause before age 40 is sometimes called premature ovarian insufficiency, and it is worth discussing with a doctor.

**How it is recognised.** In many people over 45, doctors recognise perimenopause or menopause from the history and symptoms. Blood tests are not always needed, because hormone levels fluctuate from day to day. They are more often ordered if the person is younger or the picture is unclear.

**What MenoMap does and does not do.** MenoMap cannot tell you which stage you are at. Instead MenoMap can honestly record what you notice: waves, sleep, mood and treatment, so that you and the doctor see the same picture.

backTranslations.162:
Doctors call hot flushes and night sweats **vasomotor symptoms**. A hot flush is a sudden wave of heat, often in the face, neck and chest, sometimes with redness, sweating, a rapid heartbeat or chills afterwards. Night sweats are the same thing during sleep, and can be so strong that they wake you or soak the bedding.

These are among the most common changes in the menopause period. Some people have a few mild ones, others many a day, and they interfere with work and sleep. In some they pass within a few years, in others they last considerably longer.

**What may make them more likely.** People often notice a connection with alcohol, caffeine, spicy food, hot rooms, stress or heavy bedding. This varies a lot from person to person, so tracking your own tags may be more useful than a general list.

**There can be other causes.** Redness and sweating can also be connected with thyroid problems, infections, some medications, anxiety and other conditions. If your symptoms do not fit the usual picture or are accompanied by weight loss, raised temperature or feeling unwell, tell your doctor.

**How to describe them well.** Useful details for a visit:
- Roughly how many in the day and how many at night
- How strong they are and how long they last
- Why they interfere: with sleep, work, conversations, exercise
- What seems to come before them
- What you have already tried and whether it changed anything

The "Wave" button in MenoMap and backdated entry exist precisely to record this without extra effort.

**Help exists.** There are hormonal and non-hormonal treatment options, as well as practical approaches. Which of them suit you is a question for a conversation with your doctor.

backTranslations.291:
Hormone therapy (often called HRT or MHT) replaces part of the estrogen that the body produces less of during menopause. Leading guidelines describe it as an effective treatment for hot flushes and night sweats for many people, and it can also help with other symptoms.

**It comes in different forms:** patches, gels, sprays, tablets, and also low-dose vaginal products for local symptoms such as dryness. People who have a uterus are usually prescribed a progestogen together with the estrogen, to protect the lining of the uterus.

**Benefits and risks depend on the person:** age, the time that has passed since periods stopped, personal and family history (for example breast cancer, blood clots, stroke or heart disease), and also the type of treatment and the way it is taken. That is why this is a decision made together with a doctor who knows your history, and not something an app can decide.

**Questions that are often asked:**
- Is hormone therapy suitable for me, and why or why not?
- Which type and which form would you recommend and why?
- What benefit can I expect and how soon?
- What are my personal risks and how do they compare with going without treatment?
- What should I watch for and when should we review the treatment?

**If you are already taking it,** record it in MenoMap (Profile → Medications). MenoMap will show your waves before and after you started taking it — as a coincidence check, not proof — so that at the treatment review you have something concrete to discuss.

MenoMap never suggests starting, stopping or changing medication.

backTranslations.293:
Hormone therapy is not right for everyone, and some people simply prefer other paths. There are several.

**Prescription options.** For some non-hormonal medications there is evidence that they reduce hot flushes. Among them are certain medications originally developed for other conditions, and a newer class of drugs created specifically to treat hot flushes. Each has its own advantages, side effects and interactions, so a doctor can help weigh them.

**Talking approaches and mind-body practices.** For cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) adapted for menopause there is evidence that it makes hot flushes and night sweats less burdensome and improves sleep. Clinical hypnosis has also been studied.

**Practical changes that help people:**
- Layers of clothing that can be quickly removed
- A fan by the desk and by the bed
- A cooler bedroom and breathable bedding
- Noticing and reducing your own triggers (MenoMap's tags and experiments help here)
- Regular physical activity and a steady sleep routine

**Supplements and herbal remedies.** The evidence for many of them is mixed or limited, quality varies, and some interact with other medications. Tell your doctor or pharmacist about everything you take, including over-the-counter remedies.

**Try one change at a time.** MenoMap's two-week experiments compare your own records before and during a change, and that is easier to judge than feelings.

backTranslations.416:
Most visits are short, and on the spot it is hard to recall a month of nights. People usually remember the last days or the worst ones. A simple record fills that gap.

**What a diary gives the doctor:**
- How often symptoms occur and how strong they are, not only that they exist
- Whether things are getting better, worse or staying the same
- What was happening around them: sleep, alcohol, stress, medication
- A starting point for comparison if you try a treatment

**Do not overcomplicate it.** A diary helps only if you keep it. MenoMap is built around a "Wave" button that works with one tap, and an evening summary of four questions, so it takes seconds, not a whole notebook.

**Two weeks is a good start.** Records over two to four weeks usually give a clearer picture than one bad week.

**Take your questions too.** Write down what matters most to you: the symptom that bothers you most, what you want to try or avoid, and anything that worries you. The "Visit" tab in MenoMap helps you choose questions and prints them together with the notes.

backTranslations.479:
If 12 months have passed without a period, **any vaginal bleeding must be checked by a doctor**, even if it was only once and even if it was only spotting or light pink or brown discharge.

In most cases the cause turns out to be not serious. For example, thinning of the lining of the vagina or uterus is common. But bleeding after menopause can sometimes be an early sign of a condition that is much easier to treat if it is found early. That is why health authority recommendations advise seeing a doctor rather than waiting.

**If you are taking hormone therapy,** certain bleeding can be expected depending on the type of preparation. Bleeding that is unexpected for your treatment, heavier than usual, or occurs at an inappropriate time should also be checked.

**What to do:**
- Contact your doctor or a health facility and say that you had bleeding after menopause.
- Write down the date, how heavy it was, and anything else you noticed. MenoMap can save this for you (Profile → Cycle).

MenoMap cannot tell you why the bleeding happened. MenoMap will remind you to have it checked and will add it to the visit notes.

backTranslations.529:
Poor sleep is one of the most common complaints in middle age, and rarely does it have only one cause.

**Night sweats** can wake you directly, or you become too hot or damp to fall asleep again.

**Other common factors:**
- Needing to urinate at night
- Anxiety or thoughts that will not let go
- Alcohol, which can help you fall asleep but usually makes sleep fragmented in the second half of the night
- Caffeine late in the afternoon
- Pain, restless legs syndrome or a partner's snoring
- Snoring or pauses in breathing, which can be a sign of sleep apnoea (worth telling a doctor, especially if you are very sleepy during the day)

**What usually helps.** A cool dark room; breathable bedding and layers of clothing that can be removed; a steady wake-up time; less alcohol before bed. Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is a structured, well-researched approach, and many doctors can refer you to it.

**What to track.** Over a week or two record your sleep rating, night waves, alcohol and late caffeine. MenoMap's evening summary and wave log make this a few taps. If you use an Apple Watch, MenoMap can show your sleep and wrist temperature from the Health app alongside night sweats — as context, not an explanation.

**When to get checked.** Talk to a doctor if poor sleep affects your safety (for example when driving), mood or daily life, or if you notice that at night you have pauses in breathing or gasp for air.
